F0002.rule: If tool descriptions are already clear but misrouting follows one word, look for a system-prompt instruction that ties that word to a tool. Fix that instruction. Don't pile more mechanisms on top of it.

why.A: The descriptions already state the boundaries, and misrouting follows the keyword, not the intent: the 'where's my money' wording routes correctly. That points to the system-prompt line binding the word 'refund' to `process_refund` and overriding good descriptions. Rewriting that line around intent removes the root cause with the least machinery.
why.B: Few-shot examples are a real lever for selection, but here they would compete with an instruction that still says to use `process_refund` whenever a refund is mentioned. The prompt would contradict itself, and misrouting would likely continue at some rate, because the conflicting association is still there.
why.C: This treats a selection problem as an enforcement problem. The backend already rejects these duplicate calls, so the hook only adds an earlier rejection plus a pointer to the right tool. The agent still picks the wrong tool first, and the instruction that causes it is unchanged.
why.D: Merging tools moves the choice into the `action` parameter. The system-prompt instruction tying 'refund' to issuing refunds still applies, so the agent would pick the refund action instead. The merge also bundles a read-only lookup with a money-moving write behind one interface. The guide's fix for overlap is to rename, rewrite, or split tools, not merge them.

evidence.quote: System-prompt keywords can create unintended tool associations that override good descriptions.
Descriptions are the primary selection signal. Minimal or overlapping descriptions cause misrouting.
Fix overlap by renaming and rewriting (e.g., `analyze_content` → `extract_web_results`), or split generic tools into purpose-specific ones with defined contracts.
Hooks = deterministic guarantees; prompts = probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when rules must hold.

F0002.hardness_note: This is not the official sample's setup. There, minimal descriptions made expanding them the right first step. Here the descriptions are already done, so the expected answer is ruled out and the candidate has to find a different cause. The decisive evidence is that the misrouting follows the word ("refund" misroutes, "my money" routes correctly) and that the system prompt has a matching keyword instruction. Without that detail, few-shot (B) would be defensible. The note that the backend already rejects duplicates and no money moves defuses the 'deterministic beats probabilistic' pull toward the hook (C). Consolidation (D) is tempting because the define-tools docs recommend grouping related operations, but it doesn't touch the instruction causing the problem. The options are similar in length, and the word 'system prompt' appears in both A and B, so neither wording nor length gives the key away.

F0001.rule: In hub-and-spoke orchestration, the coordinator owns all communication between agents and all error handling. If agents hand off to each other directly, the coordinator can't see failures or act on them.

why.A: This treats the symptom downstream. The returns agent duplicates the billing agent's work, the handoff still skips the coordinator, and the coordinator still closes tickets without knowing about the failure.
why.B: The failures started right after the direct queue handoff went in. The traces show the coordinator never saw the timeout, so it couldn't retry, re-delegate, or escalate, and it closed the ticket. Restoring hub-and-spoke routing gives the coordinator back control over each result and error and over what runs next.
why.C: Structured error context is the right format, but this sends it to the wrong place. Only the returns agent sees the timeout, so the coordinator, which owns error handling and ticket resolution, still marks tickets resolved without that information.
why.D: This is a detective control. The coordinator's log would record the timeout, but only after the refund is issued. The coordinator still makes no decision on the failure, so incorrect refunds and premature closures continue.

evidence.quote: Hub-and-spoke: coordinator owns all inter-subagent communication, error handling, routing (observability, consistency).
Each subagent completes its task and returns results to Claude, which then passes relevant context to the next subagent.
Subagents recover locally from transient failures and propagate only unresolved errors, with partial results and what was attempted.
Adding full production tracing let us diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically.
Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information.

F0001.hardness_note: C is the strongest distractor because structured error context is a principle the exam rewards (tasks 2.2 and 5.3). The deciding detail is that the coordinator marks the ticket resolved with nothing in its traces. That shows the error must reach the coordinator, not a peer agent. D tempts candidates who read 'no record in traces' as a logging gap, but logging after the fact changes no decision. A sounds like local recovery but fixes the wrong layer. The candidate has to combine two facts: the timing (the failures began with the direct handoff) and what the coordinator owns (error handling and resolution), which settles where the fix belongs.

F0003.rule: When the agent has the right instructions but applies them inconsistently on borderline cases, add a few targeted examples of exactly those cases that show why one action beats the alternatives. Don't add more examples, reposition the text, or force escalation.

why.A: This adds volume instead of targeting. A random sample of resolved tickets is mostly clear-cut cases, which the agent already handles 96% of the time, so the two borderline patterns stay underrepresented. The extra examples could also reinforce the existing bias toward obvious cases.
why.B: This uses a hook for a requirement that isn't a hard rule. These cases are covered by policy and all fall under the existing $500 limit, and the policy team wants most of them resolved autonomously. Forcing every one of them to a human would make the agent consistent but would hurt first-contact resolution. A hook also can't reliably judge whether a customer's account conflicts with the order record.
why.C: This fixes a retrieval problem the transcripts rule out. The agent quotes the correct clause, so it is already finding the policy text. The failure is in how it applies the clause, and moving or relabeling the text doesn't teach it how to apply it.
why.D: The policy is present and the agent is reading it, but the existing examples only show easy cases, so it has no model for the borderline judgment. A few targeted examples of these two patterns, each explaining why one action beats the plausible alternatives, generalize that judgment. Replacing existing examples rather than piling more on keeps the example set small. Drift note: the guide says 2–4 examples and current docs say 3–5. Three fits both, so the count doesn't decide the item.

evidence.quote: 2–4 targeted examples of ambiguous cases, showing why one action beats plausible alternatives.
Most effective fix when instructions alone give inconsistent format or quality.
Don't let the count decide an item. 3 satisfies both
Cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn’t pick up unintended patterns.
2–3 concrete input/output examples beat prose when prose is read inconsistently.
Triggers: customer asks for a human (honor immediately), policy exception/gap (policy silent on the case), no meaningful progress.

F0003.hardness_note: The deciding detail sits mid-stem: the agent quotes the correct clause and then applies it inconsistently. That rules out C, the lost-in-the-middle fix, and any "rewrite the policy" approach. The existing $500 hook and the under-$150 amounts are there to pull "hooks beat prompts" slogan-followers toward B. The policy team's goal of autonomous resolution and the 80% first-contact-resolution target show that B trades one problem for another. A appeals to anyone who thinks more examples are always better. Only D targets the borderline cases and the reasoning behind the choice, and it keeps the example set small.

F0005.rule: If summarization drops exact figures, take the transactional facts out of the summarized history and carry them in a persistent case-facts block. Don't try to make the summary lossless.

why.A: This fixes lost-in-the-middle, where information is present but buried. The reviewers' comparison shows the figures are gone from the summary itself, so moving the summary or adding headers can't bring them back.
why.B: Trimming tool output is a real 5.1 practice, but the 45-field lookup_order result is a red herring. The lost facts come from what the customer said, and 40+ turn sessions still get summarized after trimming. Slower growth only delays the same loss.
why.C: Correct. The failures start right after summarization, and the transcript comparison shows lossy compression of numbers, dates, and customer expectations. Keeping those facts in a persistent block outside the summarized history means every request gets them exactly, whatever the summarizer drops.
why.D: This is the slogan trap ('few-shot fixes inconsistent output'). A prompt-level fix to the summarizer was already tried and moved the error rate only one point. Summarization is still probabilistic, lossy compression, so better examples only shrink the error rate rather than guarantee exact amounts and dates.

evidence.quote: Progressive summarization loses numbers, dates, customer expectations. Keep a persistent "case facts" block outside summarized history.
Structured note-taking, or agentic memory, is a technique where the agent regularly writes notes persisted to memory outside of the context window.
overly aggressive compaction can result in the loss of subtle but critical context whose importance only becomes apparent later.
Tasks requiring precise recall of early conversation details
Lost-in-the-middle: put key findings first and use explicit section headers.
Trim verbose tool output to relevant fields (40+ fields → 5) before it accumulates.

F0005.hardness_note: Every option is a real 5.1 or 4.2 technique. Two details in the middle of the stem decide it. First, the before/after summary example shows the facts are deleted, not buried, which rules out A. Second, the failed 'retain all key figures' prompt revision shows that summarizer-side prompting doesn't fix the loss, which rules out D for anyone leaning on the few-shot slogan. The 45-field lookup_order detail is a red herring meant to pull candidates who know 'trim tool output' toward B. C is not the longest option and doesn't echo stem wording that the distractors lack.

F0004.rule: If misrouting starts right after a system-prompt change and follows a keyword rather than the request type, the cause is the prompt's keyword association. Fix the prompt wording. Don't keep piling text onto descriptions that already work.

why.A: The regression started when the system-prompt section was added. The descriptions didn't change and had held 97% accuracy. Misroutes follow the word "account", not the request type, because identical requests without that word route correctly. So the new section's broad wording has created a keyword association that overrides good descriptions. Scoping it to concrete takeover signals removes the cause.
why.B: This is the "fix the descriptions first" slogan. The descriptions were already detailed, met the 3–4 sentence guidance, and routed at 97% before the prompt change. Adding more description text leaves the conflicting system-prompt instruction in place, and that instruction is what overrides the descriptions.
why.C: Few-shot examples are a probabilistic patch stacked on top of a contradiction. The system prompt would still tell the agent to escalate account matters while the examples say not to. The root cause stays in place, and the conflict will keep surfacing with new phrasings.
why.D: This is the "hooks beat prompts" slogan used at the wrong layer. Routing on keywords in code is brittle. It would also block legitimate escalations, such as a customer asking for a human, which must be honored right away. The faulty instruction would still be in the prompt.

evidence.quote: System-prompt keywords can create unintended tool associations that override good descriptions.
Aim for at least 3–4 sentences for each tool description, more if the tool is complex.
Triggers: customer asks for a human (honor immediately), policy exception/gap (policy silent on the case), no meaningful progress.
Prompts alone have a non-zero failure rate, so deterministic compliance needs code (e.g., identity verification before financial operations).

F0004.hardness_note: Two things decide it, and both sit mid-stem. First, the descriptions didn't change and held 97% accuracy until the system-prompt section was added. Second, misroutes track the word "account": the same requests worded without it route correctly. The teammate's point that `escalate_to_human` has the shortest description is a red herring. It pulls toward B, the "fix the descriptions first" answer. D appeals to candidates who default to hooks, and C appeals to those who reach for few-shot first. The candidate has to combine "what changed" (the system prompt) with the keyword correlation to land on task 2.1's point about system-prompt keywords overriding descriptions. The C evidence quote is weaker than the others. It shows that prompt guidance is never fully reliable, which supports the claim that C leaves the conflict in place. It doesn't directly say that few-shot examples fail against a contradicting instruction.

F0008.rule: When subagents start calling each other directly, the coordinator stops seeing what happens. Bring routing and results back through the coordinator so it can see every outcome and keep the customer reply consistent.

why.A: A dedupe hook would stop the duplicate store credit. It does nothing about the second problem: the coordinator never receives the refund result, so it still tells the customer a failed refund is complete.
why.B: Both problems have the same cause. The new subagent-to-subagent path took the refund decision and its result away from the coordinator. If the refund call goes back through the coordinator, it knows a refund is in progress before it offers a credit, and it gets the non-retryable error so it can tell the customer accurately or escalate.
why.C: Merging the refund tool into the investigation subagent still leaves a refund decision outside the coordinator. That decision runs at the same time as the coordinator's work on the billing concern, so the double-resolution conflict stays. The change also hands a financial tool to a role that only needs to investigate.
why.D: Passing context happens once, when the subagent is spawned. A copy of the history made at that point can't show a credit or refund that happens afterward. It also doesn't send the refund outcome back to the coordinator, so the false success message remains.

evidence.quote: Hub-and-spoke: coordinator owns all inter-subagent communication, error handling, routing (observability, consistency).
Subagents recover locally from transient failures and propagate only unresolved errors, with partial results and what was attempted.
The only content you pass from parent to subagent is the Agent tool's prompt string, so include any file paths, error messages, or decisions the subagent needs directly in that prompt.
Tools outside an agent's role get misused.
But this asynchronicity adds challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents.

F0008.hardness_note: The stem gives two symptoms, and only B fixes both. Each distractor matches a common slogan. A fits "hooks beat prompts" and deterministically fixes the duplicate credit, but the coordinator still gets no result from the failed refund. C fits "structured errors enable recovery": the investigation subagent could see the error, but a refund decision still runs outside the coordinator alongside its billing work. D fits "pass context explicitly" but sends a one-time copy of the history at spawn. Red herrings: the 18% latency gain makes a candidate want to keep the shortcut, and the note that identity verification was clean steers away from the familiar get_customer gate. Two details decide the item. The error is already structured and non-retryable, and the coordinator received no refund result. Together they show the problem is where results go, not how errors are formatted.

F0007.rule: When the model reasons badly over a tool's raw data format, normalize that result in a PostToolUse hook before the model sees it. A gate on a downstream action only catches errors that reach that action.

why.A: A tool description is text the model reads and may or may not apply. It gives probabilistic compliance, which breaks leadership's requirement that the fix not depend on the model following instructions. The guide's advice to fix descriptions first is about tool selection, not about converting data formats.
why.B: The root cause is that the model is handed epoch seconds from one backend and misreads them. A PostToolUse hook that rewrites those fields to ISO 8601 runs in code on every legacy result before the model sees it. That fixes wrong approvals, wrong denials, and wrong deadlines at the source, and it sends no extra cases to humans.
why.C: This applies the slogan that a deterministic gate beats a prompt, and it copies the trusted $500 hook. But a PreToolUse hook fires only when the tool is called. In about 80% of the errors the agent wrongly denied or misquoted and never called `process_refund`, so this gate cannot see most of the failures. Finance's $41,000 figure is the red herring.
why.D: The legacy dates are valid data, so marking them as errors is wrong. The validation category is for bad input. Asking customers to confirm dates moves the work onto them, slows resolution on 35% of orders, and still leaves the model to read epoch values it misinterprets.

evidence.quote: `PostToolUse` hooks transform tool results before the model sees them (normalize Unix vs ISO 8601 timestamps, numeric status codes).
To replace the tool's output before Claude sees it, set `updatedToolOutput`, which works for any tool in both SDKs.
For redaction or transformation use cases, intercept at `PreToolUse` for outbound tool inputs and `PostToolUse` for inbound tool results.
PreToolUse runs only when Claude calls a tool.
Hooks = deterministic guarantees; prompts = probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when rules must hold.
Categories: transient (timeouts, unavailable), validation (bad input), business (policy violation), permission.

F0007.hardness_note: Three options are now code-level mechanisms, and two of them are hooks, so 'pick the hook' no longer gives away the answer. A follows the 'fix descriptions first' slogan, D follows the 'structured errors with isError' slogan, and C follows the 'deterministic gate' slogan by extending the trusted $500 refund hook. Without the stem, B and C are hard to tell apart. The decisive detail sits mid-stem: about 80% of the errors are wrong denials or deadlines that never call process_refund. Finance's $41,000 over-refund figure is a red herring that draws candidates toward the refund gate. The FCR/no-escalation constraint rules out D, and the 'not dependent on instructions' constraint rules out A.

F0006.rule: If the agent understands the instruction but applies it inconsistently on ambiguous cases, add a few targeted examples of those cases that show why one action beats the alternative. Don't add more prose, a hook, or a pile of generic examples.

why.A: The replays show the agent already quotes the correct clause, so it understands the prose. The problem is inconsistent application, and more qualifiers in prose leave that judgment gap open.
why.B: Correct. The instructions are understood but applied inconsistently in judgment cases. That is where few-shot is the most effective fix: a few targeted examples of exactly these ambiguous situations, each showing why one action beats the plausible alternative, teach the judgment to generalize. Three examples fits both the guide's 2–4 and current docs' 3–5, so the drift in example count doesn't affect the key.
why.C: This follows the 'hooks beat prompts' slogan, but the policy grants discretion instead of defining a rule that must hold. The amounts are small and within the existing hook limit, so a fixed rule would replace intended judgment rather than enforce a requirement.
why.D: A random sample of historical tickets is mostly routine requests, so it barely covers the three ambiguous situations and shows no reasoning about alternatives. Volume does not replace targeting.

evidence.quote: Most effective fix when instructions alone give inconsistent format or quality.
2–4 targeted examples of ambiguous cases, showing why one action beats plausible alternatives.
2–3 concrete input/output examples beat prose when prose is read inconsistently.
Hooks = deterministic guarantees; prompts = probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when rules must hold.
Cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn’t pick up unintended patterns.

F0006.hardness_note: The decisive detail sits mid-stem: the agent quotes the correct clause on every replay but decides differently. That rules out more prose (A). The $500 hook mention is a red herring that pulls slogan-followers toward C, but the policy is discretionary and the amounts are under the limit. D appeals to 'more examples is better' and fails because random sampling misses the ambiguous cases. B says 'three' examples, which fits both the guide's 2–4 and the docs' 3–5, so the drift in example count cannot decide the item.

F0010.rule: If an identity lookup returns more than one match, ask the customer for another identifier. Don't guess from context, and don't escalate a case the agent can resolve.

why.C: The root cause is that the agent picks one account when the lookup is ambiguous. The hook can't catch this because an ID does get returned. Asking for another identifier removes the ambiguity, and the agent can still resolve the case itself, so first-contact resolution is protected.
why.A: This is the failing behavior. The stem says the agent already chooses the account whose orders best fit the customer's story. Few-shot examples would train it to keep guessing from context instead of verifying identity.
why.B: This follows the slogan that deterministic beats probabilistic, but it applies it to the wrong action. Multiple matches can be resolved with one question and are not an escalation trigger. Sending about 11% of conversations to humans would push first-contact resolution further below 80%, when it is already at 76%.
why.D: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated in exactly the cases where the agent is wrong. The agent that picked the wrong account was probably confident, so a threshold would let most of these refunds through.

evidence.quote: Multiple customer matches → ask for more identifiers, never guess.
Multiple customer matches → ask for more identifiers, never guess.
Triggers: customer asks for a human (honor immediately), policy exception/gap (policy silent on the case), no meaningful progress.
Target 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
Not reliable proxies: sentiment, self-reported confidence.

F0010.hardness_note: The stem starts after the obvious first fix: the identity gate from F-Q1 is already in place, so this is a second-step item. It also includes a red herring, "the hook let the refunds through", which pulls slogan-driven candidates toward B, a deterministic hook fix that sounds right because refunds carry financial risk. Two facts in the middle of the stem decide the item. First, 11% multi-match volume combined with 76% first-contact resolution rules out mass escalation. Second, the agent already picks the account whose orders fit best, which rules out the plausible-sounding inference approach in A. D sounds like a calibration mechanism but uses self-reported confidence. Only C removes the ambiguity, keeps the case with the agent, and follows the guide's rule to ask rather than guess. The drift table has no relevant rows.

F0009.rule: An escalation handoff must carry a structured summary (customer ID, order, root cause, amount, recommended action), because the human receiving it doesn't have the agent's context and won't read the transcript.

why.A: This fits the slogan that deterministic gates beat prompts, but the stem says the agent already verifies identity before every escalation. The gate guards against a failure that isn't happening. The verified ID exists in the session but never reaches the reviewer, and a gate on the agent doesn't change what the ticket contains.
why.B: Reviewers already have the transcript one click away and seldom read 30–50 turns within a 4-minute target. Putting the same text in the ticket body doesn't change that. Humans need a short structured summary, not the raw history.
why.C: This acts on the stem's red herring. A higher limit lowers ticket volume, but the time spent on each ticket that still escalates stays the same. It also loosens a financial control that the hook currently enforces correctly.
why.D: The time goes to rebuilding context the agent already has: the verified identity, the order involved, and what went wrong. Making those fields required in the escalation tool's input means every handoff carries the structured summary a human needs to decide without contacting the shopper again.

evidence.quote: Escalation handoff = structured summary (customer ID, root cause, amount, recommended action) for humans who lack the transcript.
Block `process_refund` until `get_customer` returned a verified ID.
Pre-call interception hooks block policy violations (e.g., refunds > $500) and redirect to escalation.
Hooks = deterministic guarantees; prompts = probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when rules must hold.

F0009.hardness_note: A tempts candidates who apply "a deterministic gate beats a prompt" by reflex. It is ruled out mid-stem: identity verification already happens in every escalated session, so the gap is getting that information to the reviewer, not enforcing it on the agent. B tempts candidates who think more context always helps, and the "seldom open the 30–50-turn transcript" detail rules it out. C is the product manager's red herring: it cuts volume but not time per ticket, and it weakens a working financial control. To land on D, the candidate has to combine the scenario's handoff requirement with the evidence that reviewers are rebuilding identity, order, and root cause on their own.

F0013.rule: Give tool errors a category, a retryable flag, and a readable reason so the agent can retry transient failures, correct invalid input, and explain business rejections. A generic failure string hides all of these, so the agent can't recover.

why.A: The real problem is that the agent receives one generic string for three different kinds of failure, even though the backend already knows which kind each one is. With a category and a retryable flag, the agent can retry the 25% that are timeouts and correct the 5% over-total amounts. It can also explain the 70% policy rejections in customer-friendly terms instead of retrying them or calling them a system issue.
why.B: Backoff retries every rejection, but the stem says policy rejections return the same code on every attempt, so 70% of failures just add more multi-second waits. After all that, the agent still gets the same generic text, so it keeps calling ineligible refunds a 'temporary system issue' and keeps resubmitting over-total amounts. The vendor migration and the latency detail are red herrings that pull candidates toward fixing only the timeouts.
why.C: A retry cap in the prompt treats every failure the same and is only probabilistic. Policy rejections would still be escalated after a failed retry, and over-total amounts would still be resubmitted unchanged. The agent still can't tell the failure types apart.
why.D: This fits the 'hooks beat prompts' slogan, but it sends the 70% clear policy rejections to humans when the agent could explain them itself. That shifts work to staff and lowers first-contact resolution. A rejection under clearly stated policy is not an escalation trigger.

evidence.quote: Generic "Operation failed" prevents recovery. Return `errorCategory`, `isRetryable`, and a human-readable description. Business violations get `retriable: false` plus a customer-friendly explanation.
Write instructive error messages. Instead of generic errors such as `"failed"`, include what went wrong and what Claude should try next
Categories: transient (timeouts, unavailable), validation (bad input), business (policy violation), permission.
Tool Execution Errors contain actionable feedback that language models can use to self-correct and retry with adjusted parameters
Triggers: customer asks for a human (honor immediately), policy exception/gap (policy silent on the case), no meaningful progress.

F0013.hardness_note: The vendor migration and the multi-second gateway latency pull candidates toward B, which matches the familiar 'recover locally from transient failures' advice. B fails because the stem says policy rejections, the largest share, return the same code on every attempt. B also returns the same generic text afterward, so none of the three bad behaviors in the transcripts changes. C and D appeal to the 'cap retries' and 'hooks beat prompts' slogans but still treat every failure the same. Only A gives the agent the category information the backend already has.

F0011.rule: The loop's continue or stop decision comes from stop_reason. It continues on "tool_use" and stops on "end_turn". The presence of assistant text does not mean the turn is complete, and neither does a natural-language phrase or an iteration count.

why.A: This makes two of the guide's named anti-patterns the primary stop signal: an arbitrary iteration cap and parsing a natural-language completion phrase. The cap is a red herring. The stalled sessions ended after one response that requested a tool, not after 12 iterations.
why.B: This treats the symptom at the wrong layer, and only probabilistically. A response can legitimately contain both text and a tool call. The real defect is that the loop treats any text as completion, so the next response that happens to include narration will stall the same way.
why.C: The order service never received the call, even though the response requested lookup_order with valid arguments. So the loop exited before running the tool, most likely because it treated the narration text as a finished turn. Keying continuation on stop_reason "tool_use" and returning tool_result blocks fixes the root cause.
why.D: A PostToolUse hook fires only after a tool runs and returns. In these sessions lookup_order never ran, so the hook would never fire. It addresses a different failure: empty lookup results.

evidence.quote: In practice this reads as: while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, run the tools and continue the conversation.
Claude evaluates the current state and determines how to proceed. It may respond with text, request one or more tool calls, or both.
Anti-patterns: parsing natural-language "I'm done" signals, arbitrary iteration caps as the *primary* stop, treating presence of assistant text as completion.
are callbacks that fire at specific points in the loop: before a tool runs, after it returns, when the agent finishes, and so on.

F0011.hardness_note: The decisive detail sits mid-stem: the order service never logged the call, even though the model requested it with valid arguments. That points to the loop exiting before execution, not to a tool or data failure. The 12-iteration cap is a red herring that pulls toward A. Candidates who rely on the slogan "hooks beat prompts" are drawn to D, which can't fire because the tool never ran. B looks like a cheap fix for the narration, but it hides the loop defect instead of fixing it. The key never names the bug from the stem. The candidate has to work out that text plus a tool request was treated as completion.

F0012.rule: When one request must end in one specific tool call, force that tool by name with tool_choice. "any" still allows the wrong tool, "auto" still allows a text-only reply, and a PostToolUse hook never runs when no tool is called.

why.A: "any" stops the 8% text-only endings, but it lets the model pick any provided tool. The 3% that call `lookup_order` again would still happen and still produce no handoff.
why.B: Removing the other tools stops the 3% repeat lookups. Under "auto" the model can still answer in plain text, so the 8% `end_turn` apologies continue.
why.C: Correct. A forced `{"type":"tool","name":"escalate_to_human"}` closes both failure modes in the logs: the model can't end with a text reply (8%) or choose `lookup_order` (3%). This is the guide's mechanism for a step that must call one specific tool. Drift note: current docs say Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1, and Mythos 5.1 reject forced tool_choice with a 400. The stem pins a model that accepts it, and the exam keys per the guide (drift row 18).
why.D: This sounds like the slogan "hooks beat prompts" but uses the wrong mechanism. PostToolUse runs on tool results, and the 8% text-only replies call no tool, so the hook never fires. Resending is also a probabilistic retry, not a guarantee.

evidence.quote: `tool_choice`: `"auto"` (may answer in text), `"any"` (must call some tool), forced `{"type":"tool","name":"..."}` (must call that tool, e.g., `extract_metadata` first).
`tool` forces Claude to always use a particular tool.
`any` tells Claude that it must use one of the provided tools, but doesn’t force a particular tool.
`auto` allows Claude to determine whether to call any provided tools. This is the default value when `tools` are provided.
`PostToolUse` hooks transform tool results before the model sees them (normalize Unix vs ISO 8601 timestamps, numeric status codes).
The docs recommend `auto` + strict tool use, or structured outputs, instead. Earlier models still accept forced tool use.

F0012.hardness_note: Each option is now framed as a best practice. A cites the guide's "any" (must call a tool). B uses least privilege (remove tools this role never needs). D uses the slogan "hooks are deterministic". C is phrased as tersely as the others and is not the longest. Without the stem, A, B, and C each look like a complete fix. The decisive evidence is split and sits mid-stem: the 8% `end_turn` text replies rule out B and D (a PostToolUse hook never fires without a tool call), and the 3% repeat `lookup_order` calls rule out A. The candidate must combine both numbers to reach C. Red herrings: the teammate's more forceful prompt and the description rewrite, which pull toward the slogan "fix descriptions or prompts first". The pinned-model sentence removes the drift-row-18 ambiguity without favoring C over A.

F0014.rule: If one tool's behavior and output change depending on a mode parameter, and better descriptions and examples haven't fixed the misuse, split it into purpose-specific tools that each have a clear contract.

why.A: Correct. `lookup_order` has become a generic tool: three backends and three payload shapes sit behind one enum, so choosing the right job has turned into choosing a parameter value. The team already enriched the description and examples, and the error rate barely moved (31% → 29%). That points to the interface design, not the wording. With separate tools, each with its own name, description, and output contract, the job becomes a tool-selection choice that the agent's description-based tool selection handles well.

F0027.rule: A coordinator should choose which subagents to run based on what each request needs, not send every request through the full pipeline. A specialist that is accurate in its own domain makes noise when it is invoked on requests outside that domain.

why.A: Wrong because it follows the parallel-Task-calls guidance, but parallelism only reduces latency. Latency is already 41 s against a 90 s target, so this is the red herring. Running in parallel still invokes billing analysis on every order-status ticket, so the false duplicate-charge notes continue.
why.B: Wrong because it treats the symptom after the fact. The unneeded subagent still runs, and its output is discarded only after it is produced. Filtering on an order-status tag would also drop real billing findings on the one-in-six tickets that mix an order question with a charge question. Hooks are for rules that must hold, and the only such rule here (verification first) is not what is failing.
why.C: Wrong because it fits the 'explicit categorical criteria' guidance, but it tunes a subagent the billing team has confirmed is accurate where it belongs. Ignoring pending authorizations would hide exactly the early-duplicate signal they asked to see on real disputes. The fault is that the subagent runs where there is no billing concern, not how it judges charges.
why.D: Correct. The traces show a fixed four-subagent pipeline on every ticket, and the false findings appear only where billing analysis had nothing to examine. Letting the coordinator choose specialists per request removes that noise at the source. It still runs both order and billing specialists on mixed tickets, and it keeps the required verification-first ordering.

evidence.quote: Coordinator decomposes, delegates, aggregates, and picks which subagents to run based on the query, not always the full pipeline.
Scale effort to query complexity. Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so we embedded scaling rules in the prompts.
Decompose multi-concern requests, investigate in parallel with shared context, synthesize one resolution.
These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing Research to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems.
Hooks = deterministic guarantees; prompts = probabilistic compliance. Choose hooks when rules must hold.
